paraphrase: Found under the tulasī in Periyāḻvār's garden, Kōtai wore the garlands meant for the Lord; the Lord told her father he would accept only garlands she had worn; refusing any mortal groom, she was taken as a bride to Śrīraṅgam and entered the image of Raṅganātha.

paraphrase: Hearing the Rāmāyaṇa recited, King Kulaśekhara was so absorbed that when told Rāma was fighting fourteen thousand demons alone, he ordered his army to march to Rāma's aid; later, to prove the devotees his ministers accused of theft were innocent, he put his hand into a pot holding a cobra and was unharmed.

paraphrase: When a Cōḻa king demanded that Rāmānuja sign that nothing is higher than Śiva, Kūreśa went in his teacher's place, disguised, refused, and was blinded; Periya Nambi, taken with him, died.

The first three Āḻvārs, born of flowers at Kāñcī, Mahābalipuram and Mylapore, met one rainy night in a narrow vestibule at Tirukkōvalūr where there was room for one to lie, two to sit or three to stand; a fourth unseen presence pressed among them; Poykai and Pūtam lit their lamps of verse and in that light Pēyāḻvār saw the Lord, and the three sang the first antātis.
notes: Hagiographic account (the tradition's). Tirukkōvalūr's Lord is Trivikrama.

paraphrase: Madhurakavi found the silent youth under the tamarind at Kurukūr and tested him: 'If the small is born in the body of the dead, what will it eat and where will it lie?' Nammāḻvār answered: 'That it will eat, and there it will lie.' Madhurakavi became his disciple and served him.
notes: Hagiographic account (the tradition's). Common reading: the soul (small) born in matter (dead) lives on matter's pleasures and pains until it turns to the Lord.

paraphrase: Nāthamuni, hearing the Tiruvāymoḻi decad ending 'these ten of the thousand', sought the whole; at Kurukūr he recited Madhurakavi's Kaṇṇinuṇ Ciṟuttāmpu twelve thousand times and Nammāḻvār appeared to him and gave him all four thousand hymns with their meanings, which he arranged and set to music.

At the court of the Pāṇḍya Vallabhadeva, who sought the supreme truth, Viṣṇucitta established from scripture that Nārāyaṇa is supreme; the purse of gold hung as the prize bent down to him; the Lord appeared on Garuḍa, and the Āḻvār, fearing the evil eye on him, sang the Tiruppallāṇṭu.

paraphrase: Through Tirukkacci Nambi, Varadarāja of Kāñcī answered Rāmānuja's doubts with six sayings: I am the supreme reality; difference is the true doctrine; surrender (prapatti) is the means; the surrendered need no last remembrance at death; liberation follows at the end of this body; take Periya Nambi as your teacher.
speaker: Varadarāja (through Tirukkacci Nambi)

paraphrase: After making Rāmānuja come eighteen times, Tirukkōṭṭiyūr Nambi taught him the secret meaning of the tirumantra, charging him to keep it secret; Rāmānuja proclaimed it to all from the temple tower, saying that if he went to hell for disobedience, so many would be saved, and his teacher embraced him as 'Emperumāṉār'.

When the Pallava king banished Kaṇikaṇṇaṉ for refusing to praise him, Tirumaḻicai told the Lord of Tiruveḵkā to roll up his serpent-bed and follow; the Lord did, the city lost its lustre, the king repented, and the Lord returned when bidden — 'the Lord who did as he was told'.

paraphrase: Tirumaṅkai, robbing travellers to feed devotees, waylaid a bridal couple who were the Lord and Lakṣmī; unable to pull the ring from the bridegroom's toe he demanded the spell that held it; the Lord whispered the eight-syllable mantra into his ear, and he broke into the hymn of the name.
notes: Hagiographic account (the tradition's): the Lord himself as teacher of the mantra.

paraphrase: The pāṇar bard would not set foot on Śrīraṅgam and sang from across the river; when the priest Lokasāraṅga struck him for standing in his way, the Lord's image bled, and the Lord commanded the priest to carry the bard in on his shoulders; seeing the Lord from feet to face he sang and merged into him.

paraphrase: The Advaita renouncer Yajñamūrti debated Rāmānuja at Śrīraṅgam for eighteen days; on the eighteenth, after Rāmānuja prayed to the Lord, he conceded and became Rāmānuja's disciple as Aruḷāḷa Perumāḷ Emperumāṉār.

When Yāmuna died before Rāmānuja could meet him, three fingers of his hand remained folded; Rāmānuja vowed to write a commentary on the Brahma Sūtras, to honour Parāśara and Vyāsa, and to honour Nammāḻvār, and the fingers unfolded.
